While GPU demand remains strong, Nvidia has begun worrying about where customers will get the money to buy its chips. On August 10, Nvidia announced it would join forces with six major Wall Street financial institutions to establish a series of independent computing-power financing platforms, with plans to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital over time. The partnership targets a funding bottleneck in the GPU sales chain—if customers cannot borrow money, even surging computing-power demand will struggle to translate into actual orders. But why now? How will this financing machine operate? And if computing-power revenue proves insufficient to repay debt while GPU residual values fall short of expectations, who ultimately bears the risk?

**01 Five-year contracts underwrite GPU loans, but short-term customers are shut out**

To understand why Nvidia is bringing Wall Street into the GPU ecosystem, one must first look at the AI credit market before this initiative. According to SemiAnalysis estimates, AI-related debt balances will exceed $7 trillion by 2029, second only to the roughly $13 trillion U.S. residential mortgage financing market. Behind this massive debt demand lies the ever-expanding capital expenditure on AI infrastructure. SemiAnalysis projects that by 2028, annual AI capital expenditure (Capex) will far exceed $2 trillion, and cumulative capex from 2024 to 2029 will reach approximately $11.1 trillion. These expenditures include AI IT hardware such as GPUs, supporting CPUs, networking and storage, as well as the data centers that house them.
